content.content:
=== later
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
=== homes
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

=== near
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.
=== trail
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
=== quote
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== hischeck
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.

7033 assistant 2026-09-26T10:57:29.817Z No, it didn't fall through. There are three ways that avoid a rename. Both the clean list and the Fable judgement weighed them, and the judgement recommends against each:

1. **Stop an array's elements from being functions.** This is the spec's own design: every type parameter implicitly extends `Object`, and functions are outside `Object`. Then `fill(value)` and `fill(function)` can never be confused, and both keep the name. The compiler's own library works this way today, which is why it accepts both `fill`s. The costs:
   - Arrays whose elements are tuples stop working, because tuples aren't `Object`s either. The library's `Map`, `Heap`, sparse arrays and one team test use them.
   - Turning the bound on adds 163 new checker errors, mostly on tuples. Limiting it to the array types adds 22.
   - Steele switched this bound off in 2012 "so that interpreter tests will pass" (`c61723f61`).
   - The team's later Types chapter, which you ruled counts, puts functions under `Object`. That takes away what this way depends on.
2. **Decide at each call** (clean list ways 6 and 7). Keep both `fill`s and let each call, or a type test inside one `fill`, pick. The judgement's answer to question 1 keeps the team's rule that an overload set is checked once, where it's declared, "whether or not these calls actually appear in the program" (`advanced/overloading.tex:60-65`). The type-test version also stops checking the argument's type.
3. **Keep only the function form.** No rename, but every value fill becomes a function, for example `fill(fn (_: ZZ32): RR64 => 0.0)` instead of `fill(0.0)`. That's 7 heavier lines in microGPT's helpers.

So renaming one form is the cheapest way that keeps both forms, keeps arrays of tuples, and keeps overloads checked where they're declared. If you'd rather have no rename, the realistic candidate is way 1 limited to the arrays: it loses arrays of tuples, adds 22 errors to clear, and goes against the later Types chapter.

3:# The overload sentence, the `fill` pairs and rung N's decision 3: the judgement
20:**Question 2, `fill`: the diamond by redeclaration, the pair by two names, and it is the function form that gets the new name.** The *diamond* is `fill` inherited by an array object from two unrelated parents with no declaration below both; the library already answers that for `copy`, `map`, `ivmap` and `replica` by redeclaring in the leaf traits, and `fill` follows (18 refusals to 0, no program line touched). The *pair* is `fill(v: E)`, one value everywhere, against `fill(f: I -> E)`, a function called per index; with an unbounded element type `E`, a value can be a function, so the pair is ambiguous and the checker is right to refuse it (77 refusals). Every peer language but X10 spells the two forms differently, and wherever a peer uses the word `fill` it means the value form (Java, Scala, Kotlin, C++, Rust, Julia); where the library itself had to derive a name it put it on the function-taking form (`ivmap` beside `map`, Steele's `fill2` beside `fill`). So `fill(v)` stays and the function form is renamed; the name is Pavol's (candidates: `tabulate`, Scala's word and the mathematical one; `generate`; `fillWith`). Measured: section 9. The alternatives, in one line each: rename the value form instead (the same count, about 20 fewer lines to touch, against every peer and the library's own naming); keep only the function form, the January 2007 shape (a lambda at every value site); bound the element type so that arrays cannot hold tuples or functions (the specification's own resolution, at the cost of `Map`, `Heap`, `Sparse`, a team test, and a rule the later Types chapter reversed); change the overloading rule to decide at the call (out under question 1).

29:- Question 2 is independent of the sentence (no `fill` pair differs in static parameters) but not of the checker's model: under the paper's rules a type variable and an arrow type do not exclude, so the pair can only be separated by a name or a bound.
34:- Batch 6, beside the flattening if the manifest confirms no shared declaration, else phase 3: the `fill` rung (one library rung with its tests, the figure row, and the 12 program lines).

component TabulateRungA
export Executable

(*) explorations/compile-ladder/rung-tabulate/REPORT.md

filled[\T\](v:T): Array[\T,ZZ32\] = array[\T\](2).fill(v)

stored(x: Any): Boolean = typecase x of
    ZZ32 => false
    else => true
  end

run():() = do
  a1 = array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => i i + 1)
  assert(a1[0] " " a1[1] " " a1[2] " " a1[3], "1 2 5 10", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", 1-D")
  f1 = tabulatedArray1[\RR64,3\](fn (i:ZZ32):RR64 => 2.0 i)
  assert(f1[0] " " f1[1] " " f1[2], "0.0 2.0 4.0", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", array1 factory")
  v1 = tabulatedVector[\RR64,3\](fn (i:ZZ32):RR64 => 1.0 + i)
  assert(v1[0] " " v1[1] " " v1[2], "1.0 2.0 3.0", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", vector factory")
  s1 = array1[\ZZ32,3\]().shift(5).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)
  assert(s1[5] " " s1[6] " " s1[7], "50 60 70", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", at each index of a shifted array")
  m1 = immutableArray[\ZZ32\](3).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 7 - i)
  assert(m1[0] " " m1[1] " " m1[2], "7 6 5", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", immutable")
  a2 = array[\ZZ32\](2,3).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i + j)
  assert(a2[0,0] " " a2[0,2] " " a2[1,0] " " a2[1,2], "0 2 10 12", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", 2-D")
  f2 = tabulatedArray2[\ZZ32,2,3\](fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i + j)
  assert(f2[0,0] " " f2[0,2] " " f2[1,0] " " f2[1,2], "0 2 10 12", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", array2 factory")
  r2 = array[\RR64\](2,2).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32):RR64 => 1.0 + 2.0 i + j)
  assert(r2[0,0] " " r2[0,1] " " r2[1,0] " " r2[1,1], "1.0 2.0 3.0 4.0", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", matrix")
  a3 = array[\ZZ32\](2,2,2).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 100 i + 10 j + k)
  assert(a3[0,0,0] " " a3[0,1,1] " " a3[1,0,1] " " a3[1,1,0], "0 11 101 110", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", 3-D")
  f3 = tabulatedArray3[\ZZ32,2,2,2\](fn (i:ZZ32,j:ZZ32,k:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 100 i + 10 j + k)
  assert(f3[0,0,0] " " f3[0,1,1] " " f3[1,0,1] " " f3[1,1,0], "0 11 101 110", "row 247, array3 factory")
  c1 = a1.copy()
  c2 = a2.copy()
  c3 = a3.copy()
  assert(c1[3] " " c2[1,2] " " c3[1,1,0], "10 12 110", "arrays-distributed.tex, section \"Distributed Arrays\", copy")
  p1 = a1.map[\ZZ32\](fn (x:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 2 x)
  p2 = a2.ivmap[\ZZ32\](fn (ij:(ZZ32,ZZ32), x:ZZ32):ZZ32 => x + 1)
  p3 = a3.map[\ZZ32\](fn (x:ZZ32):ZZ32 => x + 1)

## 4. Question 2: the `fill` pairs

### 4.1 What the evidence establishes

- 95 `fill` refusals on the one library: 22 printed (in `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fsi`'s two objects) and 73 hidden behind the api's early return; 77 are value-against-function pairs, 18 the diamond. `array1(v)`/`array1(f)` and `array2` are refused by the return-type rule, not as invalid overloading, because `T` is the function's own parameter and `ZZ32 -> T` is an instance of `T` (`reviews/fill-overloads-ways.md`, the table; `captures/checker-variants.txt`).
- The diamond has one answer, the library's redeclaration in the leaf traits (`copy`, `map`, `ivmap`, `replica`, `shift`, `FortressLibrary.fsi:1420-1437`, `:1446-1461`, `:1553-1576`, "Copied here for better return type information"): measured 18 to 0.
- The pair is really ambiguous: under walk, with element type `Any`, a function passed as a value is tabulated instead of stored (`FillWalk` cases 3, 6, 7); with a function element type it is stored. The checker's refusal is the rule doing its job.
- `Vector`, `Matrix` and `vector` keep both forms because their element is bounded by `Number`, and a trait type excludes every arrow type (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:480-482`; `types-vals-vars.tex:215`).
- The specification's own resolution is the implicit `Object` bound (`trait-parameters.tex:49-50`), under which `E` excludes `I -> E`. It met reality twice: Steele switched it off in 2012 "so that interpreter tests will pass" (`c61723f61`), and measured today it adds 163 refusals, mostly tuple type arguments (the 2-D and 3-D index types), and the later Types chapter puts arrow types under `Object` (`types.tick:232-236`), which removes the exclusion the draft relied on while still excluding tuples (`:236`).
- The value form began as sugar over the function form (`fill(v:E):T = fill(fn (i:I):E => v)`, January 2007, `72ae6881b`). Where the library derived a name it derived it for the function-taking form: `ivmap` beside `map` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1178-1179`), Steele's `fill2` beside `fill` in the compiled library (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:577-579`, 2011). Peers: every one but X10 spells the forms differently; wherever the word `fill` is used it is the value form (Java, Kotlin, C++, Rust, Julia, Scala), and the function form is `setAll`, `tabulate`, `fill_with`, `from_fn`, `generate` or `init`.

### 4.2 The options, the library's own way first

Way 0 (the diamond by redeclaration) goes with each.

1. **Two names, the function form renamed.** `fill(v: E)` stays; `fill(f: I -> E)`, `array1(f)`, `array2(f)`, and for one vocabulary `vector(f)`, `Vector`'s and `Matrix`'s function form, get the new name. Commits him to a name; about 30 library call sites and the declarations; 11 test lines; the figure's function row; 12 vocabulary lines. Measured: § 9.
2. **Two names, the value form renamed** (the clean list's 3a). The same count; the value declarations and factories renamed; 15 test lines; 7 program lines. About 20 fewer lines than option 1. Against every peer's spelling and the library's own derived-name precedent.
3. **The function form only** (way 2, the 2007 shape). The value form and the value factories removed; 15 test lines; 7 program lines, each gaining a constant lambda; the figure's value row dropped; one closure call per element at allocation. Drops a convenience every peer has, and puts a lambda into `zeros`.
4. **Bound the element type** (way 1b, or 1a with the specification's switch). Keeps the figure and every program line; costs arrays of tuples (`Map`, `Heap`, `Sparse`, `ChunkedSparseArray`, `tests/sparseMatrix.fss`), 22 further refusals to clear (1b) or 163 (1a), and it rests on the arrow-outside-`Object` rule the later Types chapter reversed.
5. **Decide at the call** (ways 6 and 7). Out under question 1.

### 4.3 The decision and why

Option 1, with the diamond's redeclaration. Derived:
- *The library's practice*: the diamond has the library's one answer. For the pair, no library pattern lets an unbounded element's two forms share a name; its patterns are a bound (only where the element is a number), and a second name, put on the function-taking form both times the library needed one.
- *The type group's later word*: the checker's rule that a type variable and an arrow type do not exclude is the paper's (`exc-spec.tick:177`) and the chapter's; way 4 would keep a rule the chapter reversed and lose the tuple-indexed arrays the library is built on.
- *No open discrepancy*: the figure row changes under options 1, 2 and 3 alike; option 4 leaves the figure and changes `trait-parameters.tex` instead.
- *microGPT compiled and fast*: options 1 and 2 clear every `fill` refusal at no run-time cost; option 3 adds a closure per element at 7 allocation sites.
- *The notation*: no option touches a model line. Under option 1 `zeros(n) = array[\RR64\](n).fill(0.0)` stays as it is, and `vec(n, f)` gets the new verb.

The name: Pavol's. `tabulate` is Scala's word for exactly this and the mathematical one (the table of a function over its indices); `generate` is Haskell's and C++'s; `fillWith` is Rust's. The rung uses whatever he names.

### 4.4 What it changes

- Library: the function-form declarations in `ReadableArray`, `ImmutableArray`, `Array`, `StandardImmutableArrayType` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1299`, `:1318`, `:1338`, `:1370`) and their bodies; the way-0 redeclarations of both forms in `ImmutableArray1`, `Array1`, `Array2`, `Array3`; the factories `array1(f)`, `array2(f)`, `array3(f)` (the last takes a two-argument function for a 3-D array and is absent from the api, `FortressLibrary.fss:2830` against `.fsi:1712`, a defect row of its own); for one vocabulary `vector(f)`, `Vector` and `Matrix`; about 30 call sites (`FortressLibrary.fss:2086-2144`
- Tests: the 11 function-form lines the clean list names (`ArrayOperatorsBesideLibrary`, `vectorOps`, `ArrayScalarExtension`, `ShuffleTest`, `matrixOps`, `RandomTest`, `sparseMatrix`), plus any factory call with a function, counted by the rung.
- Specification: the function row of the arrays figure, `advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:55`, in S1's form with the original preserved; the value row stays. The comprehension notation for the function form (`comprehensions.tex:101-107`, "not yet supported") is unchanged.
